summary: Standards-track Telnet option for Linemode, where the client edits a whole line of input locally and then sends it, instead of sending each key. It was replaced by RFC 1184.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing every letter of a word one at a time, you write the whole sentence and send it at once.

questions: how does telnet linemode improve performance
subtitle: Local line editing and signal handling for Telnet over long-delay networks.

tldr.problem: Telnet usually echoes every character back to the user from the remote server, causing frustrating delays on long-distance or satellite connections and wasting bandwidth on character-by-character traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Linemode lets the client handle character editing and echo locally, buffering a complete line before sending it to the server. The RFC defines the LINEMODE option and sub-options for mode control, character settings, and forward masks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1116 became a Proposed Standard for Telnet Linemode. It was replaced and updated by RFC 1184, which consolidated linemode handling in the Telnet protocol.

today: RFC 1116 is a Proposed Standard and was updated and obsoleted by RFC 1184, which provides the current standard for Telnet Linemode. Modern Telnet implementations that support linemode follow RFC 1184, though the core concepts remain the same: local editing of input, signal translation, and negotiation of character settings between client and server.

sections.title: The Problem with Remote Echo
sections.content:
Standard Telnet sends each character the user types to the remote server, waits for the server to echo it back, and displays it on the user's terminal. On long-delay links such as satellite or intercontinental connections, this one-character-at-a-time round trip can take several seconds, making interactive typing painfully slow.

Additionally, some supercomputers are not efficient at handling single-character input; they benefit from receiving complete command lines. And networks that charge per packet penalize the high traffic of character-by-character interactions.

The RFC notes that earlier attempts to implement local line editing (like those in 4.3 BSD Telnet) used heuristics based on the ECHO and SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD options but were not reliable or complete. A clean, standard approach was needed.
sections.eli5: Waiting for each letter to go to the server and come back takes forever on slow or distant connections. Local line editing means you type a whole line on your computer, then send it all at once.

sections.title: Linemode Concept
sections.content:
Linemode Telnet divides terminal processing between client and server. The client side can enable EDIT mode, performing line editing functions like erase character, erase line, and erase word locally. The server is responsible for output processing.

The RFC identifies three operating modes of interest:

Mode 1: Local line editing and local signal trapping. The client edits the input line locally and translates special characters (like Ctrl-C for interrupt) to their Telnet equivalents before sending.

Mode 2: Remote line editing, local signal trapping. The server does line editing, but the client translates signals locally.

Mode 3: Remote line editing, remote signal trapping. Both editing and signal handling happen on the server.

Mode 1 is the most useful on long-delay networks: the user has immediate visual feedback for typing and editing, and only network delays occur when the line is completed.
sections.eli5: Linemode has three flavors. The best one for distant connections is when your computer does the editing and signal handling, so you see your typing instantly and only wait for delays when you press Enter.

sections.title: The LINEMODE Option and Suboptions
sections.content:
The RFC defines Telnet option 34 (LINEMODE) and several suboptions. The main suboptions are:

MODE: a bit mask controlling EDIT (local line editing), TRAPSIG (local signal translation), and other modes. Normally the server initiates mode changes, and the client confirms.

FORWARDMASK: a 32-byte mask of ASCII character codes that should trigger the client to forward buffered data to the server. For example, bits corresponding to space and newline would cause the client to send accumulated input when the user types those characters.

SLC (Set Local Characters): a list of octet triplets defining the local character assignments for functions like erase character, erase line, interrupt process, and end of file. Each triplet specifies a function, modifiers, and the ASCII character code to use.

The RFC also defines new control characters: ABORT (like interrupt but specifically to terminate a process), SUSP (suspend execution), and EOF (end of file).
sections.eli5: The LINEMODE option lets the client and server agree on which editing and signal functions to support, and what key each one is mapped to.

sections.title: Mode Control and Negotiation
sections.content:
When the client sends WILL LINEMODE, it requests permission to begin subnegotiation of editing and signal status. When the server sends DO LINEMODE, it requests that the client begin subnegotiation. Negotiation happens via MODE commands, each a bit mask.

The EDIT bit, when set, tells the client to perform line editing and only send complete lines. The TRAPSIG bit tells the client to translate signals like interrupt and abort to Telnet options instead of passing raw control characters.

The RFC reserves the FLOW and ECHO modes to other Telnet options (TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL and ECHO, respectively) to avoid overlap.

A client must agree with at least the EDIT and TRAPSIG state offered by the server. The MODE_ACK bit ensures both sides resolve to the same mode: if the client receives a MODE with MODE_ACK set and a mode different from current, it ignores the new mode; if the server receives such a command, it switches to the new mode.
sections.eli5: The server and client exchange MODE commands to agree on what editing and signal handling each side will do. If they disagree, the MODE_ACK bit ensures they end up on the same setting.

sections.title: Setting and Negotiating Local Characters
sections.content:
The SLC suboption allows the server and client to agree on which ASCII characters trigger which editing or signal functions. The RFC uses octet triplets: function number, level and modifiers, and character code.

Levels define whether a function is supported and whether it can be changed: SLC_NOSUPPORT (function not available), SLC_CANTCHANGE (supported but value is fixed), SLC_VALUE (supported and configurable), or SLC_DEFAULT (use the system default on the other side).

Modifiers include SLC_ACK (agreeing to a change), SLC_FLUSHIN (send a Telnet sync to flush input), and SLC_FLUSHOUT (flush output).

The RFC describes many local character functions: erase character (backspace to remove one character), erase line (clear the whole input line), erase word (remove one word), reprint line (show the current input), literal next (treat the next character literally), and flow control characters (XON and XOFF). It also defines forwarding characters that trigger immediate transmission of buffered input.

When LINEMODE is negotiated, the client either exports its local character settings to the server or imports the server's defaults, ensuring both sides agree on the meaning of special characters.
sections.eli5: The client and server agree on what key to use for "erase a character," "erase the whole line," "interrupt the process," etc. The client usually tells the server what keys it uses locally, and the server agrees or counter-offers.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that implementations do not need to implement line editing in Telnet itself; they can delegate to the system terminal driver, which handles the editing and hands the completed line to Telnet for transmission.

End-of-line handling differs between EDIT and non-EDIT modes. In EDIT mode, any normal line terminator is sent as CR LF. When EDIT is disabled, a carriage return is sent as CR NUL, and a line feed as plain LF.

When the client sends a special character that maps to an IAC function (like interrupt or abort), it must be careful not to forward prematurely if the line is still being edited. The server is responsible for all output processing and must send CR LF for newlines, CR NUL for carriage return only, and plain LF for line feed only.

The RFC requires that DO LINEMODE be sent in only one direction (by the server) to designate server and client sides. Both sides must agree on EDIT and TRAPSIG bits; the server cannot disable them, and the client cannot clear them once offered.
sections.eli5: The implementation can use the system's built-in line editor. Telnet just needs to send completed lines in the right format. Special keys that mean "interrupt" or "abort" are sent to the server as special Telnet codes, not as regular characters.
